items.text: HURRICANE THREAT - Hawaii needs to be on alert as Hurricane Lowell approaches from the southwest next week. Early indications are Lowell passes uncomfortably close to the west of Kauai next Tuesday. However, we’re talking 6 days out — and a lot can change that far out. What I do know is, Lowell will be a large and mature hurricane by that time, so major impacts especially heavy flooding rain will be felt far away from the center even if the core misses west. However, a direct major hurricane strike similar to Iniki in 1992 is on the table, so forecast trends must be closely monitored in the coming days. Stay tuned.

SOCAL COASTAL FLOODING & HIGH SURF THIS WEEKEND🌊 a Coastal Flood Advisory and High Surf Advisory are in effect Saturday through Tuesday for much of the Southern California coast as a large southerly swell generated by Hurricane Marie arrives during a period of high astronomical tides. It should be noted that Marie will NOT make landfall in Southern California but will still be powerful enough to generate the coastal flood and surf concerns.

From Ventura and Los Angeles Counties south through Orange and San Diego Counties, large waves, dangerous rip currents, beach erosion and periods of minor to moderate coastal flooding will be possible. The greatest impacts will favor south and southwest-facing beaches and other vulnerable low-lying coastal locations.

🌊 Los Angeles-Ventura: Breaking waves of 5–8 feet are expected. Coastal flooding could become most noticeable around the evening high tides - roughly 5PM Saturday, 6PM Sunday, 7PM Monday and 8PM Tuesday. Low-lying beaches, walkways and parking lots could briefly flood, with Avalon, the Alamitos Peninsula, Malibu and Point Mugu among the more vulnerable locations

🌊 Orange-San Diego Counties: Surf could reach 6-10 feet on south-southwest-facing beaches and 4-7 feet along west-facing beaches, with strong rip and longshore currents and localized coastal flooding possible

items.author: MeteorologistChristopherNunley
items.text: HIT-OR-MISS STORMS POSSIBLE ACROSS THE NORTHWEST FRIDAY⛈️a cool upper-level storm will remain over the Northwest Friday, keeping the atmosphere unstable enough for scattered showers and thunderstorms. The better thunderstorm potential stretches from western and southern Oregon into southeast Oregon, central Idaho, southeast Washington and the Idaho Panhandle. Some areas could see a few rounds of showers, with storms capable of brief heavy rain, small hail, lightning and gusty-erratic winds. With unusually cold air aloft, and the favorable placement of the low, there will also be a VERY LOW-end chance for a brief cold-air funnel or possibly landspout, particularly beneath stronger showers or thunderstorms across Oregon. This is a low probability, localized threat. Thunderstorm chances look lower across western Washington and much of western Montana, where showers will be more common than storms. This is not expected to be a widespread severe weather event, but locally heavy rain could create flooding concerns, especially across parts of Oregon and Idaho where rainfall has already been substantial⛈️

items.author: MeteorologistChristopherNunley
items.text:
RAIN & ISO. FLOOD RISK SATURDAY NIGHT-MONDAY🌧️⚠️a large Pacific storm will interact with tropical moisture from Hurricane Marie this weekend, bringing an increase in rain and thunderstorms from Southern California and the Southwest into the Great Basin and Northern U.S. Rockies. Sunday looks like the main flash-flood day across the Southwest and Great Basin. Moisture will increase across Southern California, especially the mountains and deserts, before becoming deeper across southeast California, northwest Arizona, Nevada and Utah. Utah could be one of the main areas to watch, with widespread thunderstorms and locally heavy rainfall capable of flash flooding, particularly across central and southern portions of the state.

By Sunday night into Monday, the Pacific low will start to move inland and pull moisture farther north and east into eastern Utah, western Colorado, Wyoming, Idaho and the Northern U.S. Rockies. Heavy rainfall and localized flash flooding will remain possible, especially over higher terrain and areas with saturated soils or burn scars. Idaho should see more widespread precipitation late Sunday into Monday, although current guidance favors the deepest tropical moisture passing farther south and east through Utah and Wyoming. Much cooler air will also arrive Monday, potentially bringing a rain/snow mix to the highest peaks Monday across the Inland Northwest into the Northern U.S. Rockies.

Not everyone will see flooding, and not everyone will see rain, but burn scars, slot canyons, normally dry washes and steep terrain will be particularly vulnerable to rapid runoff. The exact corridor of heaviest rain will continue to become clearer over the next couple of days🌧️⚠️

HAWAII WIND RISK INCREASING FROM LOWELL🌺🌀the greatest concern is increasingly focused on Kauai and the western end of the island chain late Monday into Monday night. While the exact track of Lowell’s northward turn remains uncertain, current guidance suggests it could move close enough to bring at least tropical-storm-force winds to portions of Hawaii. Even a relatively small shift east or west in Lowell’s eventual track could substantially change these probabilities. The latest 5-day wind-probability forecast, the chance of sustained tropical-storm-force winds from Major Hurricane Lowell has increased for parts of Hawaii, especially the western islands. The latest probabilities are around 50-60% near Barking Sands on Kauai, 30-40% near Lihue, and 10-20% near Honolulu. The probabilities rise sharply west of the islands, reflecting Lowell’s expected turn northward early next week.

It’s important to note that Hawaii is already experiencing strong, gusty trade winds, partly due to the pressure gradient between Lowell to the south and strong high pressure to the north. 3 HURRICANES ACROSS THE EASTERN & CENTRAL PACIFIC🌀🌀🌀 the Pacific is extremely active this morning with Hurricanes Marie, Karina and Lowell all spinning at the same time, and while none are currently forecast to make a direct hit [Hawaii does need to monitor Lowell closely]  on the U.S. mainland, each could influence weather from Hawaii to California and the Southwest over the coming days.

🌺 HAWAII - LOWELL IS THE BIG ONE TO WATCH: Major Hurricane Lowell is passing several hundred miles south of Hawaii, but the forecast becomes much more concerning early next week. Lowell is expected to slow and then make a sharp turn north, potentially while still a major hurricane. Lowell could move near the westernmost main Hawaiian Islands late Monday into Monday night, with the potential for wind, heavy rain, storm surge and very large surf depending on exactly where that turn occurs. Residents across Hawaii should closely monitor the forecast through the weekend and make sure hurricane plans and supplies are ready.

Hurricane Karina is farther east and is expected to eventually pass north/northeast of Hawaii. A direct impact currently appears less likely, but Karina will send a large swell toward the islands, potentially producing high-end advisory or warning-level surf along east-facing shores this weekend. With both Karina and Lowell interacting with the larger-scale pattern around Hawaii, forecast uncertainty remains elevated.

🌴CALIFORNIA & THE SOUTHWEST - WATCH MARIE: Hurricane Marie is moving west-northwest well southwest of Baja California. A direct strike on Southern California is not expected, but Marie's moisture and swells could still have noticeable impacts. Large surf is expected to reach Southern California this weekend, while tropical moisture streaming northward could increase clouds, showers and thunderstorms across portions of Southern California.

That moisture will also be drawn into the Southwest, combining with the broader monsoon pattern. Rain and thunderstorm chances increase across Arizona and eventually southeast California this weekend. The Weather Prediction Center has outlined an excessive rain risk across a good part of the Southwest as atmospheric moisture climbs well above normal, meaning locally heavy thunderstorms and isolated flash flooding will be possible🌀🌴🌧️

items.author: MeteorologistChristopherNunley
items.text:
TROPICAL TRIO OF 3 HURRICANES🌀🌀🌀the Eastern and Central Pacific remain extremely active with Hurricanes MARIE, LOWELL and KARINA all spinning at the same time!

🔴 MARIE is strengthening well southwest of Mexico and is forecast to continue generally west-northwest to northwest over the open Eastern Pacific. The storm is expected to stay well away from Mexico and the continental U.S., but moisture associated with Marie could eventually get pulled north toward parts of California and the Southwest this weekend into early next week. Again, direct impacts are not expected.

🔴 LOWELL is the monster of the three, briefly reaching Category 5 strength, about 400 miles south of Hilo. Lowell is moving west and is currently forecast to remain south of Hawaii, with no tropical watches or warnings in effect at this time. However, this hurricane needs to be monitored closely as some guidance suggest a faster northward turn, bringing impacts to Hawaii but the current forecast from the NHC does not indicate a direct impact.

🔴 KARINA remains a powerful Category 4 hurricane with 140 mph winds far east of Hawaii. It is moving west-northwest and is forecast to gradually weaken over the next several days. The NHC currently lists no direct land impacts from Karina, and there are no coastal watches or warnings in effect.

So far, none of the three hurricanes is forecast to make landfall in Hawaii, Mexico or the continental U.S., but Lowell will bring increasing surf to Hawaii and needs to be monitored closely, and Marie's moisture could eventually influence weather across portions of the Southwest and California🌊🌧️

items.author: EdPiotrowskiWPDE
items.text:
As of 5 pm on September 2, 2026 now ranks 5th on the list of latest dates for the Atlantic season’s first hurricane.

And we may not be done climbing that list.

Right now, neither the physics-based models nor the AI models show much of a signal for hurricane development over the next 10 days. If that holds, we could eventually break the record for the latest first hurricane on record.

That begs the question: Has the Atlantic ever gone an entire season without a hurricane?

Technically, yes. The 1907 and 1914 seasons have no hurricanes in the historical record. But both occurred long before the weather satellite era began in 1966. Back then, if a hurricane formed far out over the open Atlantic and never encountered a ship or land, there was a good chance no one ever knew it existed.

So while the record books say there were no hurricanes in those two seasons, it’s certainly possible there were storms spinning harmlessly over the middle of the Atlantic that simply went undetected.

I'd be fine with a big fat zero on the board for 2026!

BIG ?s WITH MARIE | RAIN FOR SOCAL & SW REGARDLESS OF TRACK🌀🌧️⛈️Tropical Storm Marie is nearing Hurricane strength in the Eastern Pacific and will soon strengthen into a Hurricane, possibly eventually a Major Hurricane! While a direct tropical storm or hurricane impact on Southern California remains very unlikely - almost 0%, Marie could still have noticeable impacts on the region this Labor Day weekend and into early next week. The key is Marie’s exact track and its interaction with an upper-level low lingering near the Pacific Northwest. The most likely scenario keeps Marie well offshore while the larger weather pattern pulls some of its tropical moisture northeastward into Southern California and eventually the Great Basin.

At this point, there is roughly a 55-65% chance of widespread light rainfall across parts of Southern California Sunday through Monday night, generally around 0.2-0.60 inches looks most probable. However, there is also about a 15-20% chance of a wetter and stormier outcome involving heavier rainfall and thunderstorms. If thunderstorms develop within the tropical moisture plume, locally heavier rainfall and flooding concerns could emerge.

There is another completely different outcome worth watching - the dry side. If the pattern develops differently, and Marie remains well offshore, gusty offshore, easterly winds could develop ahead of the moisture that could increase fire-weather concerns in parts of Southern California before any rainfall arrives. This only has about a 10-15% chance of happening.

So, long story short, there is still a fairly wide array of possibilities, but the most probable is for light to moderate rain occurring across parts of Southern California this weekend into early next week. The important point is that Marie does not have to make landfall in California to influence the weather. Even hundreds of miles offshore, its moisture can be pulled northward into the region. 

Small changes in Marie’s track could make a significant difference in how much moisture ultimately reaches Southern California so expect the forecast to continue changing as Marie strengthens and its track becomes better established over the next few days🌀🌧️⛈️

items.author: GregDeeWeather
items.text:
A new study published last month highlights the Gulf Stream's variability.

The study looked at satellite data over a 31-year period from 1993 to 2024 and found the Gulf Stream intensified significantly from 2014 to 2023. This was preceded by a period of Gulf Stream weakening from 2005-2014. 

The study shows the Gulf Stream is not constant and goes through periods of higher & lower activity. The study was an observational one & did not look at why these changes were happening, but the variation is part of a larger ocean current system known as the "subtropical gyre." 

The Gulf Stream transports heat from the southern latitudes to the North Atlantic & the higher latitudes, increasing heat release to the atmosphere & warming the upper ocean.  

They found that when weaker, the portion of the Gulf Stream in the North Atlantic flows farther south, leading to colder & drier winters across Europe. A stronger Gulf Stream flows farther north, leading to wetter & warmer winters in Europe, especially western Europe.    

The study shows how complicated & dynamic Earth's ocean current system is, making it difficult to describe & generalize in simple rules or statements. 

Very interesting!   

Study info: https://www.aoml.noaa.gov/satellite-data-reveals-gulf-stream-intensification/

items.author: GulfCoastUpdates
items.text:
AROUND THIS TIME 18 YEARS AGO, #Gustav made landfall along the #Louisiana coast near Cocodrie as a Category 2 hurricane.

It came just three years after #Katrina, and Gulf Coast anxiety couldn't have been any higher... everyone was on edge.

While Gustav was still in the Caribbean as a Category 4, New Orleans mayor Ray Nagin called it "the storm of the century."

Thankfully, it wasn't the storm of the century, but it did still pack a major punch.

First and foremost, it was the first massive evacuation of SE Louisiana since Katrina — about 2 million people left the Louisiana coast ahead of landfall.

Storm surge of 10-14 ft hit parts of Louisiana's coast. It caused an estimated $6-7 billion in damage in the United States.

While I was working at the TV station in Baton Rouge from 2011-2014, I spoke to many locals who said Gustav was the worst storm they had ever been through there.

It was yet another example that the "category" of a storm doesn't always tell the whole story. Even though Gustav was "only" a 110 mph Category 2 at landfall in Louisiana, the impacts proved how dangerous lower-category hurricanes can still be.

EL NIÑO GIVETH, AND EL NIÑO TAKETH AWAY

One of the classic hallmarks of El Niño is a tale of two oceans...a very busy tropical Pacific and a relatively quiet Atlantic. Extremely warm water and light wind shear in the Pacific are helping fuel tropical activity, while El Niño has brought relentless wind shear and sinking air to the Atlantic, making it very difficult for tropical storms and hurricanes to develop and strengthen.

Right now, the Pacific is loaded. There are two major hurricanes and a tropical storm nearing hurricane strength. Hurricane Lowell is on the verge of Category 5 intensity with 155 mph winds, while Hurricane Karina is a Category 4 with 145 mph winds. Tropical Storm Marie is also forecast to become a hurricane soon. None of these systems are a threat to Hawaii. 

Meanwhile, over in the Atlantic...crickets. Not a single system is expected to develop over the next seven days.

Quite the tale of two oceans!

items.author: EdPiotrowskiWPDE
items.text:
Long before Mom passed away, Cindy and I made spending time with our parents a priority. We’re blessed to have both of our families here in Myrtle Beach, and we’ve always known how precious that time is. With Mom confined to a wheelchair, she especially loved when Dad or we would take her out for breakfast, lunch or dinner. Looking back, I’m so grateful for those seemingly ordinary moments because today they mean everything.

Tuesday morning, Cindy and I had breakfast with Dad at Zeytin. Nothing fancy, no special occasion, just breakfast together. But these are exactly the moments we cherish even more now. Since Mom passed, we’ve been spending more time with Dad, Momma Linda and Papa Wade. Not out of sympathy or obligation, but because losing Mom reinforced something we already knew: you never get time back, and you never know how much of it you have with the people you love.

That realization has really affected me personally. I find myself thinking about my mortality far more than I used to. I’ll turn 60 in December, and sometimes I struggle with just how quickly life seems to be passing. I’ve spent years telling people to take life one day at a time, and now I’m realizing just how hard it can be to take my own advice.

So when those thoughts creep in, I turn to Cindy and we lean on our faith. Jesus says in Matthew 6:34, “Therefore do not worry about tomorrow, for tomorrow will worry about itself. Each day has enough trouble of its own.” And Psalm 90:12 says, “Teach us to number our days, that we may gain a heart of wisdom.” Maybe numbering our days isn’t about worrying how many we have left, but appreciating the one we have today.

I can’t control how much time I have, and worrying about it certainly won’t give me any more. What I can do is make the most of the time God gives me...to love Cindy, cherish Dad, Momma Linda and Papa Wade, spend time with the people who matter most, and keep making memories.

I’m trying to leave tomorrow with God and be thankful for today. I know that’s what I need to do. But knowing it and actually doing it are two very different things.

MARIE & SOUTHERN CALIFORNIA: SEVERAL LABOR DAY WEEKEND OUTCOMES REMAIN POSSIBLE🌀🌧️⛈️Tropical Storm Marie has formed in the Eastern Pacific and is expected to strengthen into a Hurricane. While a direct tropical storm or hurricane impact on Southern California remains very unlikely - almost 0, Marie could still have noticeable impacts on the region this Labor Day weekend and into early next week. The key is Marie’s exact track and its interaction with an upper-level low lingering near the Pacific Northwest. The most likely scenario keeps Marie well offshore while the larger weather pattern pulls some of its tropical moisture northeastward into Southern California and eventually the Great Basin.

At this point, there is roughly a 55-65% chance of widespread light rainfall across parts of Southern California Sunday through Monday night, generally around 0.2-0.60 inches looks most probable. However, there is also about a 15-20% chance of a wetter and stormier outcome involving heavier rainfall and thunderstorms. If thunderstorms develop within the tropical moisture plume, locally heavier rainfall and flooding concerns could emerge.

There is another completely different outcome worth watching - the dry side. If the pattern develops differently, and Marie remains well offshore, gusty offshore, easterly winds could develop ahead of the moisture that could increase fire-weather concerns in parts of Southern California before any rainfall arrives. This only has about a 10-15% chance of happening.

So, long story short, there is still a fairly wide array of possibilities, but the most probable is for light to moderate rain occurring across parts of Southern California this weekend into early next week. The important point is that Marie does not have to make landfall in California to influence the weather. Even hundreds of miles offshore, its moisture can be pulled northward into the region. 

Small changes in Marie’s track could make a significant difference in how much moisture ultimately reaches Southern California so expect the forecast to continue changing as Marie strengthens and its track becomes better established over the next few days🌀🌧️⛈️

items.text: ISOLATED T-STORMS THURSDAY FOR PWN⛈️behind Wednesday’s strong fall-like storm system, colder air aloft will settle over the Pacific Northwest on Thursday! Combined with daytime heating, this will create an unstable environment supportive of scattered convective showers and-or isolated thunderstorms, especially Thursday afternoon. These are expected to be mostly weaker, pop-up thunderstorms rather than organized severe storms, so the overall severe weather threat remains low. However, any stronger thunderstorms could produce dangerous lightning, brief heavy rain, gusty and erratic winds and small hail. Given the position of the surface low to the PNW coast, an isolated cold-air funnel cloud or waterspout also cannot be ruled out but tornadoes are NOT expected. The unsettled weather will continue beyond Thursday as the upper-level low lingers over the region. Periods of showers and isolated storms could persist Friday into the weekend. Keep in mind, as always, NOT EVERYONE sees storms - they will be isolated in nature, but if a storm approaches, please move indoors⛈️

CENTER INTERCEPT! I normally don’t go after tropical storms or low end hurricanes so this was a first of a kind outing for me today. 

Edouards tiny size and only 4 mile wide eye (at times) made it a challenge. They eye got flung around insure what looked like a bigger eye, making positioning for the landfall tricky, but pulled it off.

What really surprised me about this one was the intensity of western eyewall. In most tropical systems it’s usually the right front quadrant that gets the most intense winds, but not this one. It seemed to strengthen after making landfall continuing to produce gusts as high as 90mph 2 hours after the fact.

All in all a useful day out in the field. It’s really a good thing the storm had a short time over water, that final hour or so before landfall it really slipped a switch and began cranking. A unique storm, and one that’s good to learn from. 

Parts of Texas and Louisiana are a little messy and without power, but thankfully nothing worse! Thanks to everyone who shared important weather info to their family friends and neighbors!

There will be a threat for storms (of which could be strong to severe) beginning in the morning. The most active time frame, however, should favor the afternoon and evening Wednesday. Early action manipulates & affects action later in the day, so it'll be a forecast of constant change and evolution with regard to how things ultimately play out. A relatively quiet first half of the day likely yields storms with more bite into the second half. We'll take things one step at a time. 

Bottom line, we have many severe weather days in WNY. This will be one of them. Sometimes, we get off easy with no issues and other times parts of the area have some cleaning up to do. Days like this aren't necessarily uncommon or unusual, but when they are in the forecast it is wise and prudent to make sure you are weather-aware and paying attention to any headlines that could arise. Given the fact there is a small chance of tornadic development, a little front end planning could go a long way, even if the odds of something like that impacting you are limited.
